questions.question: What is Amazon CloudWatch primarily used for?

options.text: Storing application data
Monitoring metrics, logs, and events from AWS services
Managing IAM users and permissions
Deploying containerized applications

explanation.correct: CloudWatch is AWS's native monitoring and observability service that collects metrics, logs, and events.
explanation.why: A is S3, C is IAM, D is ECS/EKS.

questions.question: At what CPU utilization percentage should you treat an EC2 instance as effectively at full capacity?

explanation.correct: 80% CPU utilization is effectively full capacity because the OS cannot efficiently schedule and move tasks around beyond this point.
explanation.why: Waiting for 100% means the system is already failing. 80% is the industry best practice threshold.

questions.question: What are the two main types of data CloudWatch collects?

options.text: Events and Alerts
Metrics and Logs
Reports and Dashboards
Traces and Spans

explanation.correct: CloudWatch collects Metrics (numerical data points over time) and Logs (text records of events).
explanation.why: Events and alarms are CloudWatch features built on top of metrics, not the primary data types.

questions.question: What does an HTTP status code in the 500 family indicate?

options.text: The request was successful
The client made an error in the request
The server encountered an error processing the request
The resource was permanently moved

explanation.correct: 500-family codes indicate server-side errors — the service itself has a problem processing the request.
explanation.why: 200 = success, 4xx = client error, 301/302 = redirects.

questions.question: Which CloudWatch feature allows you to search and analyze log data using a query language?

options.text: CloudWatch Alarms
CloudWatch Dashboards
CloudWatch Log Insights
CloudWatch Events

explanation.correct: CloudWatch Log Insights is an interactive query tool that lets you search and filter log data using a SQL-like query language.
explanation.why: Alarms trigger notifications, Dashboards visualize data, Events responds to changes.

questions.question: What is a Unix epoch timestamp counting from?

options.text: January 1st, 2000
January 1st, 1970
January 1st, 1980
The current system boot time

explanation.correct: Unix epoch time counts seconds (or milliseconds) elapsed since January 1st, 1970 at 00:00:00 UTC.
explanation.why: This convention was established with the original Unix operating system in 1970.

questions.question: When does CloudWatch display timestamps?

options.text: In the user's local timezone
In EST (Eastern Standard Time)
In UTC (Coordinated Universal Time)
In PST (Pacific Standard Time)

explanation.correct: CloudWatch stores and displays all timestamps in UTC. Users must convert to their local timezone when analyzing logs.
explanation.why: UTC provides a universal reference that avoids daylight saving complications across global teams.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between CloudWatch and CloudTrail?

options.text: CloudWatch is free; CloudTrail costs money
CloudWatch monitors performance and logs; CloudTrail audits API calls
CloudWatch is for EC2 only; CloudTrail covers all services
CloudWatch stores data forever; CloudTrail deletes after 7 days

explanation.correct: CloudWatch monitors operational metrics and application logs; CloudTrail records API calls and tracks who did what in your AWS account.
explanation.why: Both cover all AWS services. Both have costs. CloudTrail keeps 90 days in event history by default.

questions.question: Where do logs from services like S3 and many AWS managed services often get stored besides CloudWatch?

options.text: DynamoDB
RDS
Amazon S3
Amazon EBS

explanation.correct: Many AWS services store logs in both CloudWatch Logs and Amazon S3, giving flexibility in how they are accessed and analyzed.
explanation.why: S3 is the primary object storage for large-scale log archival and integration with analytics tools like Athena.

questions.question: What HTTP status code indicates a successful API call?

explanation.correct: HTTP 200 indicates success — the server received, understood, and processed the request successfully.
explanation.why: 404 = Not Found, 500 = Server Error, 301 = Redirect.

questions.question: What CloudWatch AI feature, launched globally in August 2024, automatically analyzes log query results and identifies patterns?

options.text: CloudWatch Anomaly Detection
AI Summarize Results in Log Insights
CloudWatch Contributor Insights
CloudWatch ServiceLens

explanation.correct: The AI Summarize Results feature in CloudWatch Log Insights was trialed in June 2024 and launched globally in August 2024.
explanation.why: Anomaly Detection uses ML for metric baselines. Contributor Insights analyzes who contributes to metrics. ServiceLens is for distributed tracing.

questions.question: What do the majority of log entries from an always-on SageMaker model endpoint consist of?

options.text: User prediction requests
Error messages
Keep-alive health check pings
Billing events

explanation.correct: Always-on SageMaker endpoints generate constant health check keep-alive pings to confirm the compute is still running, which constitute the majority of log entries.
explanation.why: This is why AI summarization is valuable — it filters out keep-alive noise to surface meaningful events.

questions.question: Why is generative AI unreliable for converting Unix epoch timestamps?

options.text: AI models don't have access to the internet
AI models predict likely text rather than performing precise arithmetic
Unix timestamps are encrypted and AI cannot decrypt them
AWS restricts AI from accessing timestamp data

explanation.correct: LLMs work by predicting statistically likely output, not by performing mathematical calculations. Timestamp conversion requires precise arithmetic that LLMs fabricate plausibly but incorrectly.
explanation.why: This was directly demonstrated in class — the AI confidently provided wrong dates for log events.

questions.question: What is an inference profile in Amazon Bedrock?

options.text: A user preference file that customizes AI responses
A load-balancing mechanism that distributes model requests across multiple endpoints
A billing profile for model usage
A security profile that controls who can invoke models

explanation.correct: An inference profile is essentially a load balancer that distributes requests across multiple instances of an AI model, either within a region (US/EU) or globally.
explanation.why: Large models like Claude Sonnet require inference profiles — direct model invocation is not supported.

questions.question: A developer is using a global inference profile and experiences severe timeouts during a regional outage. What is the most effective immediate mitigation?

options.text: Increase the API timeout setting in the application code
Switch to a regional inference profile for an unaffected geography
Upgrade to a larger EC2 instance
Enable CloudWatch detailed monitoring

explanation.correct: Switching from a global to a regional inference profile limits routing to data centers in a functioning geography, bypassing the impacted region.
explanation.why: Timeout settings don't fix infrastructure unavailability. EC2 size doesn't affect Bedrock routing. CloudWatch monitoring helps diagnose but doesn't fix routing.

questions.question: What does a 13-digit Unix timestamp represent compared to a 10-digit timestamp?

options.text: A newer format with higher security
Milliseconds since epoch instead of seconds since epoch
A timestamp from after the year 2001
A timestamp in a different timezone

explanation.correct: A 13-digit Unix timestamp counts milliseconds since January 1, 1970, providing millisecond-level precision. A 10-digit timestamp counts seconds.
explanation.why: CloudWatch uses millisecond precision (13 digits) to allow precise event sequencing within busy systems.

questions.question: When troubleshooting an AI application with CloudWatch, latency metrics show spikes but the logs show no application errors. What should you check next?

options.text: Restart the EC2 instance immediately
The AWS Service Health Dashboard for known infrastructure incidents
Increase the model's memory allocation
Delete and redeploy the model endpoint

explanation.correct: When application code appears fine but performance degrades, the problem is often infrastructure-level. The AWS Service Health Dashboard shows known incidents affecting AWS services.
explanation.why: This was exactly the scenario in class — the latency spikes were caused by infrastructure problems in affected regions, not application bugs.

questions.question: You have a Bedrock application serving European healthcare users. An outage affects your EU-West region. Which approach is MOST problematic?

options.text: Failing over to another EU region
Failing over to a US region
Using a global inference profile as fallback
Both B and C

explanation.correct: Failing over to a US region may violate GDPR data residency requirements. Using a global profile that routes to non-EU regions has the same problem for regulated healthcare data.
explanation.why: GDPR and HIPAA can restrict which regions are legally permitted for specific types of user data.

questions.question: In CloudWatch Log Insights, you want to find all log entries where the response code was 500. Which query structure is correct?

options.text: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE code = 500
fields @timestamp, @message | filter @message like /500/ | sort @timestamp desc
GET logs WHERE statusCode == 500
FIND @message CONTAINS '500' IN logs

explanation.correct: CloudWatch Log Insights uses its own query language with commands like fields, filter, sort, and limit — not standard SQL syntax.
explanation.why: The Log Insights query language uses pipe (|) to chain operations, similar to Unix command piping.

questions.question: What is the key difference between a Log Group and a Log Stream in CloudWatch?

options.text: Log Groups store metrics; Log Streams store text
Log Groups contain Log Streams; a Log Group is per-application, a Log Stream is per-source
Log Streams are for real-time data; Log Groups are for historical data
Log Groups are free; Log Streams incur charges

explanation.correct: Log Groups organize all logs from one application or service; within a Log Group, Log Streams hold the sequential events from individual sources like specific EC2 instances or model variants.
explanation.why: This hierarchy makes it possible to isolate logs from specific components within a larger application.

questions.question: You have three data centers in the Middle East within 300 miles of each other, plus one in Paris. You call this a 'multi-region' architecture. Why might this still create a single point of failure?

options.text: Because three data centers are always worse than one
Because a regional event could disable all three Middle East locations simultaneously
Because AWS only counts geographic regions, not data centers
Because Paris has higher latency than Middle East regions

explanation.correct: Geographic proximity means that regional events — geopolitical, natural, or infrastructure-related — can affect multiple data centers simultaneously, eliminating the redundancy benefit.
explanation.why: True redundancy requires geographic separation sufficient that a single event cannot affect all locations at once.

questions.question: What is the difference between CloudWatch observing 'Keep-alive 200 OK' vs 'Invocation 200 OK' in SageMaker logs?

options.text: There is no meaningful difference
Keep-alive confirms compute is running; Invocation confirms the model processed a user request successfully
Keep-alive is for serverless models; Invocation is for dedicated instances
Keep-alive uses GET requests; Invocation uses DELETE requests

explanation.correct: Keep-alive pings (GET requests) confirm the compute infrastructure is still running. Invocation calls (POST requests) confirm the model actually processed a user request. A service can be 'up' on keep-alive but failing on invocations.
explanation.why: This distinction is critical — keep-alive success doesn't guarantee model functionality.

questions.question: A cloud architect argues: 'We have data in Bahrain AND Paris, so we have full redundancy.' A Middle East conflict takes Bahrain offline. What is the actual state of their redundancy?

options.text: They are still fully redundant because Paris is available
They effectively have single-region deployment in Paris only, despite believing they were redundant
They have zero availability because Bahrain is the primary region
They automatically fail over to a third AWS region

explanation.correct: With Bahrain offline, all traffic and data falls to Paris alone. Their 'multi-region' design is now effectively a single-region setup, with no failover capacity if Paris also has issues.
explanation.why: This was exactly the scenario AWS was communicating to customers about during the Middle East infrastructure disruptions.

questions.question: A CloudWatch investigation shows latency spikes at 08:39 and 08:42 UTC. The engineer is in Pacific Time (UTC-7). What local times correspond to these events?

options.text: 3:39 PM and 3:42 PM
1:39 AM and 1:42 AM
1:39 PM and 1:42 PM
8:39 AM and 8:42 AM

explanation.correct: UTC-7 means Pacific time is 7 hours behind UTC. 08:39 UTC minus 7 hours = 01:39 Pacific. So the events happened at 1:39 AM and 1:42 AM Pacific time.
explanation.why: Wait — 08:39 UTC - 7 hours = 01:39, which is 1:39 AM. Be careful with UTC conversions. If it was 08:39 Pacific that should appear as 15:39 UTC.

questions.question: Why would CloudWatch show a validation exception error from a Bedrock model invocation but not reveal the exact line of code causing it?

options.text: CloudWatch automatically hides security-sensitive error details
CloudWatch sees network-level traffic but not internal application code execution details
Bedrock encrypts all error messages before sending to CloudWatch
Validation exceptions are not logged by Bedrock

explanation.correct: CloudWatch captures what crosses the network — request/response codes and surface-level messages. Application-internal errors (wrong model ID in code, logic bugs) require application-level debug logs, not CloudWatch.
explanation.why: This is why you need multiple monitoring layers: CloudWatch for infrastructure-level visibility, application logs for code-level debugging.

questions.question: An AI application uses a global Bedrock inference profile. During normal operations this provides the best latency worldwide. When would you consider switching to a regional profile?

options.text: Only when explicitly required by AWS support
When regulatory requirements mandate data residency in specific geographies
When cost is the primary concern
Both B and when specific regions experience infrastructure outages

explanation.correct: Regional profiles should be used when data residency regulations require keeping traffic within specific geographies, OR when specific regions are experiencing outages and you want to isolate from them.
explanation.why: Global profiles offer broader capacity but expose you to any region's problems. Regional profiles trade coverage for isolation.

questions.question: You're building a log analysis tool with AI. Your tool correctly identifies error patterns but reports wrong timestamps for when they occurred. The AI says errors happened on January 15th but logs clearly show March 24th. What is the most likely root cause?

options.text: The CloudWatch API returned incorrect data
The AI model is guessing/fabricating timestamp conversions from Unix epoch format
The application has a timezone configuration bug
UTC and local time conversion is failing

explanation.correct: LLMs cannot reliably convert Unix millisecond timestamps to human-readable dates and will fabricate plausible-sounding dates. The correct fix is to use a programming language's date library for conversion before passing data to the AI.
explanation.why: This exact scenario was demonstrated in class with the instructor's custom log analysis tool.

questions.question: The AWS Service Health Dashboard shows 'All Systems Operational' but your CloudWatch metrics show high latency for a Bedrock model. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: CloudWatch metrics are delayed by 24 hours
The health dashboard is always wrong during incidents
Your specific account or resources may be experiencing issues not yet reflected on the public dashboard, or the issue is in application logic
Bedrock is not covered by the AWS Service Health Dashboard

explanation.correct: The public health dashboard shows broad service status. Account-specific issues, partial degradation, or rapidly emerging incidents may not immediately appear. Additionally, application-level issues show as latency in CloudWatch but not infrastructure health.
explanation.why: Always check both the public dashboard AND your personal health dashboard for your specific resources.

questions.question: A SageMaker model endpoint returns a 500 error in under 1 millisecond. What does this ultra-fast failure time tell you?

options.text: The model processed the request extremely quickly
The failure occurred in a preprocessing layer before the model even received the request
The 500 error was caused by a network timeout
The model's GPU accelerator failed

explanation.correct: If a model invocation fails in 0-1 milliseconds, the model itself never processed the request. A preprocessing validation layer (checking request format, content type, etc.) rejected it before it reached the model.
explanation.why: This was demonstrated in class — sending a non-image to an image classification model failed instantly at the preprocessing layer, not the model layer.

questions.question: Your team wants to use CloudWatch AI Summarize for production log analysis. Which scenario represents a valid limitation you must account for?

options.text: AI Summarize only works on logs from the last 24 hours
AI Summarize cannot identify patterns when there are fewer than 100 log entries
AI Summarize may surface patterns and suggest mitigations but cannot tell you the root cause of infrastructure-level outages beyond what is in the logs
AI Summarize is only available in the us-east-1 region

explanation.correct: CloudWatch AI Summarize is powerful for identifying patterns in logs, but it can only reason about what is in the logs. External causes (geopolitical events, hardware in other regions) appear only as error codes and timeouts — not as root cause explanations.
explanation.why: This is why you combine CloudWatch with the AWS Health Dashboard and external context to complete the full picture.
